title: Sitting with someone
hook: Job's friends sat with him seven days and said nothing; why the rabbis built the shiva rule from the wrong friends
tomorrow: in the old Greek story, why did hope stay in the jar?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: call out. Job cursed his day, Ayyub named his trouble, and both were answered. Today, the ones who came when he cried.

On the drive over to see someone who got terrible news, people rehearse. What do I say? Here's an odd thing in the Book of Job. Job's three friends are the ones who get it wrong: by the last chapter, God is angry with them. Yet the rabbis took a rule for comforting mourners straight from those same three men. How? Look at their first week. They see him and barely know him. They weep and throw dust on their heads. Then: "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him."
screen: `WHAT DO I SAY?` → `THE WRONG FRIENDS.` → `SEVEN DAYS. NONE SPAKE A WORD.`

segments.voice: The verse finishes: "for they saw that his grief was very great." The friends were wrong when they talked. They were right while they were silent. And notice who breaks the silence: Job. He opens his mouth first, and only after that does Eliphaz answer. That order became law. The Talmud, in the tractate Moed Katan, teaches that comforters may not say a word until the mourner speaks first, and it learns the rule from Job. Jewish mourning keeps its own seven days, called shiva, Hebrew for seven. When a close relative dies, mourners sit shiva: they stay home, they sit low, and friends come to sit near them and bring food. So the puzzle solves itself. Jewish practice kept the friends' silence and left their speeches behind. And look where the trouble starts: the long argument that fills the book begins when the comforters begin explaining. Under the custom is a teaching any path can use: presence before explanation. You don't have to fix the grief or justify it. You go, you sit at their height, and you let them speak first. The speeches can wait. Some never need to come.
screen: `RIGHT WHILE SILENT.` · `THE MOURNER SPEAKS FIRST.` · `SHIVA: SEVEN DAYS.` · `PRESENCE BEFORE EXPLANATION.` · then, large: `THE FIRST SEVEN DAYS.`

segments.voice: Lower yourself: sit on the floor, or on the lowest seat near you, the way mourners sit at shiva. Let your hands rest open. Bring to mind one person carrying something heavy, and stay there with them, saying nothing at all.
Sitting with someone: going to them and staying near, without speeches. Job's friends got this part right, for seven days.
Pocket this one: the first seven days, when the friends said nothing and got it right. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jewish mourners sit shiva, traditionally for seven days after the burial of a close relative; visitors come to the house, sit near them, and by custom wait for the mourner to speak first (Moed Katan 28b, learned from Job).
